In the theory of [[Spectrum (topology)|spectra]] in mathematics, a '''Morava E-theory''' (also called '''Lubin–Tate theory''' or '''Johnson–Wilson theory''') is a particular spectrum or equivalently [[Generalized cohomology theory|generalized (co)homology theory]]. For a [[prime number]] <math>p</math> (obmitted in notation), these form a sequence <math>E(n)</math> of spectra, hence one for each [[natural number]] <math>n\in\mathbb{N}</math>. Morava E-theories form the foundation of [[chromatic homotopy theory]], in which a spectrum is separated into so-called (mono)chromatic layers by using its various Bousfield localizations with respect to the different Morava E-theories, so-called chromatic localizations <math>L_{E(n)}</math>. Morava E-theory is named after [[Jack Morava]], who introduced it in unpublished preprints in the 1970s.

== Definition ==
For a [[perfect field]] <math>\mathbb{K}</math>, hence in which every [[irreducible polynomial]] is [[Separable polynomial|separable]], of characteristic <math>p</math>, let <math>W(\mathbb{K})</math> be its ring of [[Witt vector|Witt vectors]].<ref>Hopkins 1999, Definition 16.4</ref> Let <math>R=W(\mathbb{K})[v_1,\ldots,v_{n-1}]</math> be the [[polynomial ring]] in <math>n-1</math> variables, called Lubin–Tate ring. According to [[Landweber exact functor theorem|Landweber's exact functor theorem]], a [[formal group law]] over the Lubin–Tate ring defines a [[generalized cohomology theory]], which according to [[Brown's representability theorem]] is represented by a spectrum, which is Morava E-theory <math>E(n)</math>. It fulfills:

: <math>\pi_0E(n)
=R[\beta^{\pm 1}]</math>

for its ring of coefficients with <math>\beta\in R</math> in second degree.

== Properties ==

* The chromatic localization <math>L_{E(n)}</math> preserves [[Smash product|smash products]].<ref>Lurie 2010, Lecture 22</ref>
* <math>E(n)</math> is Bousfield equivalent to <math>E(n-1)\times K(n)</math>.<ref>Lurie 2010, Lecture 23</ref> (<math>K(n)</math> is [[Morava K-theory]]. Two spectra are Bousfield equivalent, when their [[Generalized homology theory|generalized homology theories]] vanish on the exact same [[Topological space|topological spaces]]. Hence for every topological space <math>X</math>, one has <math>E(n)_*(X)=0</math> if and only if <math>E(n-1)_*(X)=0</math> and <math>K(n)_*(X)=0</math>.)
* <math>E(n)</math> is <math>K(n)</math>-local.<ref>Lurie 2010, Lecture 35</ref> (<math>K(n)</math> is [[Morava K-theory]]. <math>K(n)</math>-local means that every spectrum morphism <math>X\rightarrow E(n)</math> from a <math>K(n)</math>-acyclic spectrum <math>X</math> is [[nullhomotopic]]. <math>K(n)</math>-acyclic means that <math>K(n)\wedge X\simeq 0</math>.)
* A connected [[Closed manifold|closed]] [[Spin manifold|spin]] 10-manifold is generalized oriented in second Morava E-theory <math>E(2)</math> (for <math>p=2</math>) if and only if its seventh integral [[Stiefel–Whitney class]] <math>W_7</math> vanishes.

== E(n)-local spheres ==
For the [[sphere spectrum]] <math>\mathbb{S}</math> (with <math>\mathbb{S}_n=S^n</math>), its chromatic localizations <math>L_{E(n)}\mathbb{S}</math> are also called <math>E(n)</math>-local spheres.
